articles.title: A stab in the back: Why an AfD victory in Saxony could pose a national security threat to Germany
articles.body:
For the first time in its history, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has a real chance of forming a regional government. On Sept. 6, voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will go to the polls, and experts are already describing scenarios in which the AfD would have enough votes to govern alone. In that case, the German political system’s “firewall” — the voluntary commitment of other parties not to cooperate with the radical right — would prove powerless. The AfD’s rise to power even in a state as small and economically weak as Saxony-Anhalt could cause serious problems for Berlin — including in the key areas of defense and security.
The “plan for Germany” is under threat
In Germany, a regional government cannot directly influence the nation’s foreign or defense policy. This is the exclusive prerogative of the federal center, in the form of the Bundestag and the government. That said, the AfD makes no secret of its opposition to weapons deliveries to Ukraine and to broader European rearmament plans. The party describes Berlin’s actions as a “course toward war” and demands “the restoration of partnership with Russia.”
Even if a party representative were to take the premier’s seat in Magdeburg, they would be unable to change Germany’s current geopolitical course. Moreover, the authors of Germany’s Basic Law anticipated the possibility of conflict between the federal center and a state, embedding protective mechanisms in two separate articles.
Article 37 allows the federal government to apply coercive measures in the event that local authorities refuse to follow a national decision. Additionally under Article 85, the federal government may issue direct instructions to the states within the framework of so-called “federal supervision.” But the process isn’t simple.
If an event in Europe were to trigger NATO’s Article 5 mechanism, Germany’s civilian authorities and military would begin implementing the Operational Plan for Germany (OPLAN DEU) — a set of mobilization and logistics measures that include the redeployment of large military contingents and equipment from western and southern Europe to the east, and Berlin’s allies would be counting on the use of German territory as a key hub for defensive operations. Although the exact routes for convoy movements are classified, several factors suggest that Saxony-Anhalt has been assigned an important role in such plans.
First, the geographic location of the state is perfect, as it sits halfway between the western part of the country and Poland. As a result, virtually the only route for a rapid response runs through Saxony-Anhalt. After all, numerous key Bundeswehr bases and logistics centers are located in and around the state.
Second, this region has in recent years undergone large-scale rehabilitation of its rail network, autobahns, and secondary roads. Many of them are now considered to be among the best in Germany. Plans through 2029 call for further modernization of the central rail hubs in Magdeburg and Dessau, as well as capacity expansion on the Magdeburg–Berlin route.
A state government, if it chooses, could significantly slow down military convoy movements at precisely the moment when every hour counts. For example, a hypothetical premier of Saxony-Anhalt who opposes “escalation” and calls for “seeking compromises at the negotiating table” could refuse to issue the permits required for heavy — and especially tracked — military vehicles to pass through the region, as the issuance of such permits falls within the competence of the relevant state authority. In addition, military convoys are required to move exclusively with a police escort whose purpose is to close off civilian traffic, and law enforcement agencies are subordinate to local authority.
A state government could significantly slow down military convoy movements at the very moment when every hour counts
Finally, decisions about the use of regional infrastructure — such as allocating land for tent camps and ensuring supplies of electricity, water, and fuel — are made locally, not at the federal center. Even the exchange of information between central command structures and the operations hub in Magdeburg could be significantly hampered.
There is no doubt that in an emergency, Berlin would immediately invoke its powers under the relevant articles of the Basic Law, and it is also fair to assume that not every senior police officer would agree to openly sabotage defensive measures. But precious hours — or even days — could still be lost, creating grave ramifications for the defensive strategy of both Germany individually and NATO as a whole.
Red tape as a weapon
The reputation of German bureaucracy is renowned far beyond the country’s borders. On one hand, the meticulous observance of the letter of the law and strict adherence to procedure guarantee a functioning rule-of-law state, reducing the actual power of those in positions of authority.
On the other hand, what makes the system stable simultaneously renders it vulnerable to legalistically legitimate, functionally pointless legal challenges. Although the AfD’s core political demands are unachievable without the approval of the Bundestag and the federal government, authorities at the state level possess all of the necessary mechanisms to make life considerably more difficult for the chancellor and their ruling coalition in Berlin.
A state is a significant player on Germany’s political field. The Bundesrat, the chamber of the states, approves nearly 40% of the laws passed by the Bundestag — and that approval is far from automatic. Since the Federal Republic’s founding in 1949, the Bundesrat veto has been used more than 100 times.
Moreover, some initiatives approved by the government and the upper house of parliament — such as recent payments to the public that required co-financing from the states — were never unblocked. And even though Saxony-Anhalt has only four of the Bundesrat’s 69 seats, this by no means implies legal weakness.
Presently, AfD parliamentary groups in the Bundestag and the state parliaments frequently pressure the executive and legislative branches with a barrage of motions, bills, and inquiries. These often lack any legal basis, but the system is obliged to respond to them.
For the AfD, this is an opportunity to demonstrate activity to its voters and convince them of its own effectiveness as the “only genuine opposition.” Moreover, around 7,000 AfD inquiries concerning the state of critical infrastructure and the country’s defense between 2020 and 2025 raise serious concerns among politicians and journalists.
Armed with votes in the Bundesrat and a new lever of influence, the AfD could well push this process to the point of absurdity, creating tangible stress for government administration. A state is what is known as a “constitutional body,” meaning it has the right to file a complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. Under the unwritten rules of the game, a state government hardly ever resorts to this instrument — only in cases where the state’s rights have been seriously violated and numerous mediation councils with the federal center have yielded no result.
Statistically, state lawsuits account for just 1% of all cases examined by the Constitutional Court, and referrals to the court to review the legality of a given federal law are almost as rare — in the range of two to three per year. However, there are no legal limitations on the number referrals that can be submitted, meaning that a state under AfD rule could well disregard the unwritten rules and flood the Constitutional Court with challenges to any law passed by the Bundestag. The focus would be, first and foremost, on the issues most sensitive to a radical electorate: the entry and residence of foreign nationals, refugee admissions, environmental policy, and funding for renewable energy development, gender equality programs, and measures to strengthen European unity.
A state under AfD rule could flood the Constitutional Court with challenges to any law passed by the Bundestag
Blocking tax legislation would also theoretically be possible, posing a potential threat to the smooth functioning of the country’s fiscal system. Admittedly, federal laws are not subject to suspensive effect — meaning their entry into force would not be suspended on account of a pending complaint. Still, a mass attack on the Constitutional Court would inevitably affect its productivity and, indirectly, the functioning of government bodies.
A state also has the right to file a so-called urgent application, which would indeed effectively block a law until a final decision is reached. As a rule, the Constitutional Court grants such an application only in exceptional cases of serious harm to the state and its residents, but here there is ample room for legal interpretation and hairsplitting.
Finally, while four seats in the Bundesrat represent a mere 3% of the total membership, even these could become a “golden share” under certain conditions. The AfD’s appearance in the Bundesrat as the ruling party in its state would further legitimize the far-right party, and in the event of a serious conflict between states or a deadlock in the body, one side might not be able to resist the temptation to form a temporary alliance with the AfD in order to secure victory in the dispute with the help of Saxony-Anhalt’s votes.
Reshaping the system
The intense focus of foreign — and indeed many German — observers exclusively on federal politics is understandable. The state level may seem dull and unimportant, but in Germany’s federalist model the region plays a significant role in the implementation of policy. The state commands numerous levers of government administration, and here, the AfD would obtain tangible opportunities to change a great deal if it were to come to power.
All school-level education, along with a significant share of higher education, is a state-level responsibility. In Germany, a teacher is not required to follow the textbook to the letter and enjoys considerable freedom in shaping lesson concepts, but a hypothetical AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt would be quite capable of reformatting the educational process.
The party’s attention is focused primarily on the subject of “history,” and it makes no secret of its rejection of the form of historical memory and perception of past events that has developed in the Federal Republic. Instead, it would prefer a departure from the sense of guilt — or more precisely, collective responsibility — of the German people for the crimes of Nazism, as well as from the negative assessment of the militarism of the Second Reich, the colonial period, and a number of historical figures from the last 150 years.
Ideally, the AfD wants to foster the development of German patriots who are proud of their country and do not dwell on the dark pages of its history. This approach could be reflected in new curricula, which teachers are not entitled to ignore.
The AfD wants to raise German patriots who are proud of their country and do not dwell on the dark pages of its history
The state Ministry of Education would also be able to exert sufficient administrative and financial pressure on schools and universities to shut down initiatives aimed at combating racism, xenophobia, homophobia, and sexism. The AfD has an extremely negative attitude toward gender equality and diversity, feminism, and the use of gender-neutral language, meaning all of these could become a thing of the past in the area under its authority.
Admittedly, under such a scenario, the human factor would play a considerable role. Would thousands of teachers, officials, and administrators be willing to comply with the new rules of the game? This is where the second important set of state-level powers comes into play: personnel policy. Saxony-Anhalt has approximately 115,000 public-sector employees — 12% of the entire working-age population — and in a region with high unemployment, low wages, and very poor prospects on the open labor market, some administrators may choose to adapt to the new realities rather than risk being dismissed. In the five years before the next elections, the AfD could well appoint “ideologically compatible” personnel to senior and mid-level positions. This also applies to the state Center for Political Education, an important government body promoting democracy, which the new government could restructure beyond recognition.
Finally, the state government controls the police and the Office for the Protection of the Constitution — the body that, back in November of 2023, classified the AfD’s state organization in Saxony-Anhalt as “definitively right-wing extremis.” Should the AfD come to power, it may be tempted to exact revenge on the agency. Meanwhile, the state police have already been mired in scandals on multiple occasions involving the discovery of racist and antisemitic messages in internal chats, while year after year, human rights activists record an increase in cases of police brutality.
Even worse, it is not inconceivable that some local police officers would welcome “a firm hand” in power. In addition, the state Interior Minister has the authority to block individual law enforcement operations, and a hypothetical AfD minister would undoubtedly make use of that privilege.
Not least, the emergence of an AfD-led government even at the state level would deal a crushing blow to the firewall. Germany’s Basic Law explicitly requires the states to cooperate with one another. Without this, German federalism would simply be unworkable. In practice, the regions are genuinely bound by political ties — from the Bundesrat, where the mode of cooperation is different from that in the neighboring chamber of parliament, to the format of joint conferences of relevant state ministers. Currently, such conferences are held in 21 areas — from meetings of state premiers to forums of interior, economics, justice and transport ministers.
The AfD’s rise to power in Saxony-Anhalt could provide the final contribution to the “normalization” of the far-right party on a wider scale.

articles.title: US deputy defence chief to visit NATO HQ, Patriot systems for Kyiv may be discussed
articles.body:
US deputy defence chief to visit NATO HQ, Patriot systems for Kyiv may be discussed
Elbridge Colby, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, is visiting NATO headquarters in Brussels on 27 August as part of US plans to review its military presence in Europe, according to sources. The issue of providing Ukraine with interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems may also be raised.
Source: European Pravda, citing sources in NATO and diplomatic circles
Details: The main topic of Colby's visit to NATO on 27 August is the US military presence in Europe, although military assistance to Ukraine may also come up during the discussions.
"The United States is holding consultations with allies as part of a review of the deployment and structure of its forces. The US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy will take part in a meeting of the North Atlantic Council tomorrow as part of these ongoing consultations," a NATO official told European Pravda's Brussels correspondent.
Sources in Brussels diplomatic circles also confirmed to European Pravda that the main purpose of the North Atlantic Council meeting on 27 August is to discuss the review of the deployment and structure of US forces in Europe.
Nevertheless, NATO diplomats said the issue of Ukraine could be raised during discussions with the US official.
European Pravda has also learned that another meeting of the North Atlantic Council at ambassadorial level took place on Wednesday 26 August, during which issues concerning Ukraine were among the topics discussed.
Participants at the meeting discussed the urgent need to provide Ukraine with more military assistance, particularly PAC-3 interceptor missiles and Patriot systems, which are currently among its most pressing needs.
Financial assistance to Ukraine was also discussed, including funding to cover the shortfall in the country's defence budget.
Background:
- Colby is visiting NATO headquarters in Brussels on 27 August.
- The US Department of Defense is currently reviewing its military presence in Europe, which could pave the way for a reduction in the number of US troops on the continent.
- CIA Director John Ratcliffe recently visited Moscow and, according to some reports, warned Russian officials against escalating tensions with US NATO allies, particularly Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

articles.title: How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualised
articles.body:
On 28 February 2026, the US and Israel began large-scale strikes on Iran. Tehran responded by attacking Israeli and US allies across the Gulf.
Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, was killed on the first day of strikes, and the strait of Hormuz – a crucial waterway for transporting oil – was effectively closed soon after. The conflict quickly became a regional war with global economic consequences.
Since then, bursts of fighting have repeatedly given way to ceasefires and negotiations. Each diplomatic opening has been followed by fresh threats, disputed agreements and renewed attacks.
The strait of Hormuz remains at the centre of the conflict. In normal times, more than 100 vessels passed through the narrow waterway each day, carrying about a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade. Any closure or attack on shipping can disrupt global supplies and send prices higher.
This timeline traces six months of strikes, public threats and failed diplomacy - and shows how the war has disrupted shipping and driven swings in the oil price.
Methodology
The Guardian looked at about 4,000 Truth Social posts, 7,700 IRGC Telegram messages and a selection of X posts from 28 February 2026. Some social media posts have been edited for conciseness. All times included in the piece are GMT.
Oil price data is sourced from LSEG. Data on the amount of shipping traffic through the strait of Hormuz is sourced from Lloyd’s List Intelligence, and only includes traceable transits of cargo-carrying vessels over 10,000 deadweight tonnage. Dark transits included in figures after 28 Feb.
Airstrikes data is sourced from Acled, and includes data on explosions or remote violence events, including air/drone strikes and shelling, artillery and missile attacks, by the Iranian, US and Israel military forces. It excludes interceptions.

articles.title: Russia lashes out at UK, France over Ukraine missile technology transfer
articles.body:
Russia lashes out at UK, France over Ukraine missile technology transfer
Moscow warns of potential strikes on British military targets, urging London to change its stance on supporting Kyiv
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Thursday that Russia could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.
Zakharova called on Britain to back off what she called London’s hostile stance on Ukraine, which she said risked taking the conflict to an entirely new level.
She had told the same Moscow news briefing earlier that Britain and France were “playing with fire” by supplying sensitive missile technology to Ukraine.
Britain announced on Monday it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to licence the technology for the European missile.
Also on Thursday, the Kremlin dismissed US media reports that Russia could attack a Nato member state and that the purpose of US CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow this week had been to warn Russia against such a move.
Asked to comment on the reports, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said: “A lot of this kind of scare-story material is being published right now. Of course, it has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation.”

articles.title: CIA Director gives Kremlin intelligence on Russian losses that Putin not being told — NYT
articles.body:
CIA Director gives Kremlin intelligence on Russian losses that Putin not being told — NYT
According to Ukrinform, this is the explanation for Ratcliffe’s visit presented by The New York Times, whose authors cited current and former U.S. officials.
According to the newspaper’s sources, the CIA doubts whether Putin is receiving accurate information from his advisers about the course of the war and Russia’s losses.
Ratcliffe reportedly made it clear to FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov that, given the difficult military and economic situation, Moscow should begin serious negotiations to end the war.
At the same time, Ratcliffe reportedly made no threats or warnings about possible consequences from the United States if Putin ignored the intelligence assessment and decided to continue the war.
According to the NYT, the communication channel between Ratcliffe and Bortnikov operates in parallel with other contacts between the Trump administration and Kremlin representatives, including through presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Some U.S. officials hope that Putin, who himself worked in intelligence, will regard the CIA director’s message as more urgent and credible than if it had been delivered through ordinary diplomatic channels.
The NYT notes that Russia’s battlefield offensive has stalled and Russian forces are suffering significant losses. In July, Ratcliffe publicly stated that the average life expectancy of a Russian serviceman on the front line was less than 35 minutes.
He also said that during his 18 months as CIA director, Russia had captured only about 1% of Ukraine’s territory. Ukraine’s effective use of drones significantly hindered the Russian offensive.
According to the NYT, before meeting with Bortnikov, Ratcliffe spoke with his Ukrainian counterparts and assured them that during his visit he would determine Russia’s position and would not negotiate any concessions on Ukraine’s behalf.
During previous contacts, Ratcliffe and Bortnikov had discussed details of prisoner exchanges, but their meeting in Moscow this week was their first face-to-face meeting.

articles.title: Trump says Iran is 'in deep trouble' as US maintains blockade of Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump addressed Iran’s situation on Thursday evening, saying that “Iran right now is not paying its soldiers. They are in deep trouble. They have very little capability left.”
Trump also discussed the Strait of Hormuz and US activity in the area, saying, “Last night we moved 24 ships through the strait. We move them all the time. I’m saying this openly.”
He said, however, that the military activity had not ended, adding, “As you know, the Strait of Hormuz is open. We have control and we have a blockade. Iran is getting nothing. Nothing is going through. No ship is going through.”
Asked whether he would punish Russian President Vladimir Putin or Russia if Moscow continued trading with Iran, Trump said the response would depend on the circumstances.
“Up to now, I think Russia has behaved pretty well when it comes to the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
Russia won't attack NATO territory, Trump affirms
Trump also addressed Russia during his remarks to reporters, following the visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to the country two days earlier.
Asked why Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed or committed not to attack NATO territory, Trump responded, “I had good conversations with him. He is not going to attack NATO territory.”
Asked whether he had warned Putin not to do so, Trump said, “I don’t want to comment on that, but they are not going to attack.”
Trump was also asked why he had not imposed sanctions on Chinese banks that conduct business with Iran. He responded, “Who said I’m not? You’re asking ‘why not,’ who said? You don’t know if I’m doing it. I don’t have to announce everything, right?”
Addressing the possibility of renewed talks with Iran, Trump said, “We don’t want to talk to them. We’re not looking to meet or something like that. The strait is open, we are moving a lot of ships. Millions and millions of barrels of oil are going through the strait every day.”
He also said the US had completely cleared the Strait of Hormuz of mines, adding, “We have the best minesweepers in the world.”
Trump said the US was closely monitoring Iran through its Space Force, saying, “We see every inch of the strait. Every ship that enters with a mine, we see it and destroy it. We have already destroyed two of them.”
Meanwhile, sources familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal that the Trump administration has repeatedly made clear to mediators that it has no interest in returning to the terms of the memorandum of understanding signed with Iran in June.
According to the sources, the position has complicated efforts underway this week to restart diplomatic negotiations.
According to the newspaper’s report, the initial agreement signed by Trump at Versailles, with Vice President JD Vance involved in its formulation, was intended to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and launch negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program and an end to the war, in exchange for sanctions relief.
Although Trump has said he ultimately wants an agreed-upon end to the confrontation, he is currently willing to wait and assess whether increased economic pressure on Tehran will produce results.
The approach follows the administration’s launch this week of a broad economic campaign aimed at cutting off the Iranian regime’s sources of revenue and financial connections.

articles.title: Russia says it could strike UK military targets in response to Kyiv's use of British missiles
articles.body:
Russia says it could strike UK military targets in response to Kyiv's use of British missiles
MOSCOW, Aug 27 - Russia warned on Thursday that it could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukrainian attacks on targets inside Russia using long-range British cruise missiles.
The warning, delivered by Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova at a news briefing in Moscow, was the strongest of is kind yet from Russia to Britain, a NATO member state and a staunch ally of Ukraine.
Zakharova said London was "one step away" from becoming legally complicit in what she called "terrorism" against Russian civilians, something she said would have "catastrophic consequences" unless Britain changed course.
"We have repeatedly warned that any British military installations and equipment in Ukraine and beyond its borders could be targeted in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory carried out using British weapons," she said.
"We propose that the British leadership once again carefully analyse the situation and immediately, in the most resolute and unequivocal manner, abandon the hostile, aggressive line, which can only ... create the risk of the conflict escalating to an entirely new level," she said.
Zakharova issued her warning a day after Russia accused Ukraine of firing British Storm Shadow missiles at a shopping centre in the Russian-controlled city of Donetsk in eastern Ukraine in an attack which it said wounded civilians, including children.
The Kremlin said on Monday that Britain was methodically adding "fuel to the fire" after London announced it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to license the technology for the European missile. REUTERS

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.
The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.
“The stop is a routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.
Earlier this week, the Thai navy said that three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify the vessels or provide a date.
The planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeks amid reports of poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. The Navy Times also reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.
On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard told MS Now that her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.
Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which is defined as someone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.
The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” which is when the service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.
The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.
The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.
The navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. In a statement to MS Now about the decision to pursue a non-judicial punishment for the sailor, a navy official said that “the Navy is fully committed to the health and wellbeing of every Sailor”.
“We strive to foster environments that support mental health by removing barriers to seeking help, increasing awareness of resources, and taking appropriate action when someone is in need,” they added. “Mental health resources are available to our Sailors 24/7, and asking for help is a sign of strength.”
The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 November bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than 250 consecutive days without a significant port visit.
Reports about the conditions onboard have prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.

articles.title: Trump’s war on Iran is rapidly draining US navy budget, documents and interviews reveal
articles.body:
Donald Trump’s war on Iran has driven the US military into a severe financial crisis, with the US navy forced to transfer money from its payroll and other sources to cover the costs of combat, according to documents obtained by the Guardian, and interviews with navy officials, contractors and defense analysts.
The US-Israeli operation, which has depleted US munitions stockpiles and prompted retaliatory Iranian strikes that have wrecked strategic bases across the Middle East, is piling pressure on budgets across the military.
One Pentagon memo about navy funding seen by the Guardian warns that there are “shortfalls in payroll” accounts due to the department “raiding” them to fund combat operations.
Experts and former officials say the accounts are running dry. “The piggy bank is broken,” said Harlan Ullman, a retired naval officer. Ullman is a member of the National Commission for the Future of the Navy but he said he is not speaking on the commission’s behalf.
One official and one navy contractor said non-emergency maintenance on shore-based facilities has been deferred because of the cash crunch.
When Trump started the war on 28 February, it quickly strained the military’s existing budgets – particularly that of the navy, which not only helped launch the initial wave of attacks but was later responsible for an extensive naval blockade. The White House eventually asked Congress for emergency funding to pay for the war efforts, but prospects that the request will be approved are dim amid the unpopularity of the war.
A navy official who was briefed on how the service is planning to address the shortfalls said money is shifted around in imaginative ways. “The money for payroll,” he said, “was robbed to pay for overseas contingencies and is being backfilled by money that hasn’t been spent. They are backfilling payroll so we get enough money in our paycheck.”
The navy’s budget for 2026, almost $300bn, has different batches of money allocated by Congress for various requirements: personnel, shipbuilding, procuring specific weapons systems and “operations and maintenance”, the day-to-day running of the fleet and its bases. The law limits how money can be rejiggered throughout all those batches of money.
The issue has occasionally surfaced in some hearings on Capitol Hill. Susan Collins, in a 21 July hearing of the Senate appropriations committee, said: “I’m told some military services face near-term solvency challenges.” A staffer said the navy was one of the services Collins was referring to.
In a statement, a navy spokesperson said maintenance and operations funds have not been depleted. “The Department of the Navy,” the statement said, “is actively managing its resources to meet current pay obligations on time. We continue to work closely with Congress to address ongoing operational demands and sustain our personnel and readiness throughout the fiscal year.”
Inside the service, the cash shortage is no secret. “They’re just not speaking publicly about it,” said Todd Harrison, a defense analyst at the conservative American Enterprise Institute. “And I suspect that is a deliberate decision of the civilian leaders in the Pentagon, starting at secretary, that this is for political reasons, that they don’t want to look like they’re damaging future military readiness over a war that is becoming increasingly a political liability.”
‘We face critical shortfalls’
The military knew the crisis was coming. In mid-May, Adm Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, cautioned Congress that the crunch would hit in July. “The FY ’26 budget didn’t bake in Epic Fury,” he said. “I do fear that I’ll have to start making decisions in the July timeframe on how I do force generation. That could make differences between how I do exercises, how I do routine operations in order to make sure that I … have the funds necessary to continue the war effort for Epic Fury.”
Pete Hegseth has pushed Congress for emergency funding, without which, he said in July, “we face critical shortfalls”. The defense secretary testified that the Iran war cost $35.7bn, but it’s unclear if that is a full accounting of the war’s costs.
When the Trump administration asked Congress for $67bn in emergency funds for the defense department, it didn’t break down how much would be for the navy. The House passed a $1.15tn defense bill in July and a separate budget authorization that would provide $73bn for the war in Iran, but it’s unlikely either will become law.
Ullman noted that during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, funding was more forthcoming from Congress because those conflicts were authorized by a resolution. “There is no authorization to use force in this case. Is Congress obliged to pay for a conflict it did not authorize?” he said.
‘They ran out of their money’
The fact that the navy is broke – or at least out of money for now – may be something of a slap in the face for Trump.
The president has often evoked what he sees as his affinity with Theodore Roosevelt, who was president from 1901 to 1909 and presided over the expansion of the US navy, deploying the so-called “Great White Fleet” that steamed around the world. Instead of a Great White Fleet, Trump’s administration has embraced the term “Golden Fleet”. Among his naval ambitions: plans for mammoth “Trump class” ships – the largest battleships in US history.
Trump’s micromanagement has included directing the navy to redesign an aircraft carrier so it launches jets with a steam and hydraulic catapult system rather than by an electromagnetic system. As the Guardian reported, every year since 2017 he has opined about his preferences in carrier launch catapults.
At this point, however, funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challenge. A former military officer now working for a navy contracting company, who has been briefed on the shortfalls, said: “They’re fucked. They shot all their weapons; they trashed all their ships; they ran out of their money.”

articles.title: CIA Chief Told Kremlin Russia’s War Is Going Badly – and Putin May Not Know It, NYT Says
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe used a secretive trip to Moscow this week to deliver a bleak assessment of Russia’s war against Ukraine, warning that Moscow’s military and economic position would deteriorate further if the Kremlin refused to pursue serious peace negotiations, The New York Times reported Thursday.
Ratcliffe delivered the warning directly to Aleksandr Bortnikov, head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to current and former US officials cited by the newspaper.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The unusual intelligence mission sought to deliver the assessment through a channel that could carry particular weight with Russian President Vladimir Putin. CIA analysts have long questioned whether Putin’s advisers are giving him an honest picture of the war’s trajectory and the scale of Russia’s battlefield losses.
US officials reportedly hoped Putin, himself a former Soviet intelligence officer, would take a message from the CIA director more seriously than one delivered through traditional diplomatic channels.
Stalled advances and massive losses
Ratcliffe’s assessment emphasized the enormous price Russia has paid for limited territorial gains in Ukraine.
The warning echoed public comments by the CIA director last month, when he said the life expectancy of a Russian soldier on the front line was “less than 35 minutes” and that Moscow had captured only about 1% of Ukraine’s total territory during the previous 18 months.
Explosions Heard in Kyiv as Russian Jet-Powered Drone Heads Toward City Center
Ratcliffe attributed Russia’s meager advances to Ukraine’s “mastery” of drone technology.
The assessment marks a striking shift from assumptions held by President Donald Trump and some of his senior advisers last year that Russia’s larger population and nuclear arsenal made an eventual battlefield victory over Ukraine inevitable.
Instead, Russian forces have suffered massive losses while their battlefield gains have largely stalled.
Ratcliffe reportedly told Bortnikov that, given Russia’s increasingly bleak military and economic outlook, Moscow should enter serious negotiations to end the war before its position worsens further.
Kremlin confirms secret talks
The Kremlin confirmed that Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday and held talks with senior Russian intelligence officials but did not meet Putin.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin had been briefed on the outcome of the meetings but declined to disclose what was discussed.
Russia’s foreign intelligence chief Sergei Naryshkin also confirmed that he met Ratcliffe during the visit, describing the talks as a working-level meeting.
Trump has publicly played down the unusual intelligence mission, calling Ratcliffe’s trip “semi-routine” while suggesting that direct intelligence contacts could contribute to efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The visit was the first known trip to Moscow by a CIA director since November 2021, when then-CIA chief William Burns traveled to Russia months before Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: NATO discusses Russian escalation towards Ukraine and Alliance member states
articles.body:
NATO discusses Russian escalation towards Ukraine and Alliance member states
During a meeting of the North Atlantic Council attended by Elbridge Colby, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, at NATO headquarters in Brussels on 27 August, officials discussed Russia's hostile escalation towards Ukraine and NATO member states.
Source: Deputy Polish Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski, who took part in the discussions, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The officials discussed Russian escalation towards Ukraine and NATO's allies with Colby.
"We talked about the last few weeks of escalation that is taking place on the part of Russia in Ukraine but also towards the European countries. We agreed on the nature of Russian policy and the threats that Russian policy poses to NATO," Zalewski said.
He stressed that the US is "pursuing a wise policy of responding appropriately rather than discussing it publicly". According to Zalewski, Poland has "a very similar view when it comes to the threat posed by Russia in the context of Ukraine and in the context of NATO".
Quote: "I expressed my deep conviction that the formula that the Americans have adopted, the formula that NATO is implementing, is not based on verbal protests but on real capabilities that are important from a military point of view and show the possibility of blocking any aggressive Russian actions."
Details: In his view, the right approach is to "create real strategic dilemmas for Russia and show them the limitations that are related to NATO capabilities", rather than engage in discussions.
Zalewski also described the central topic of his conversation with Colby at NATO as "common security issues in the context of the Pentagon's strategy to strengthen the North Atlantic Alliance through the implementation of the NATO 3.0 plan".
Quote: "The 3.0 plan is based on the idea that a large number of conventional defence duties are to be placed on European countries. The United States is to provide support for key military capabilities, leadership, and of course political and military leadership. Poland is a supporter of this way of thinking. We have been investing in our own capabilities for several years now."
Background:
- Zalewski also said that Poland seeks to begin producing PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot systems on its territory and is ready to cooperate with Ukraine in this area.

articles.title: Ukraine hit more than 200 civilian vessels this year – Moscow

Ukraine hit more than 200 civilian vessels this year – Moscow
Ukrainian forces have hit 214 civilian vessels flying the flags of various countries in the Black Sea since the start of the year, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
Speaking at a regular briefing on Thursday, Zakharova lashed out at Ukraine, arguing that Vladimir Zelensky’s “regime continues to create military threats for the states of the Black Sea region.”
She pointed to a string of attacks on commercial shipping near Russian ports this month, including several raids on vessels operated by Turkish companies. Ukrainian drones hit the San Marino-flagged Necibe. Its 18 crew members were rescued by the Turkish-owned vessel Ural, which was also later struck by Ukrainian drones, leaving one Turkish citizen dead and eight other people injured.
“Here we see how the weapons procured and transferred to the Kiev regime through NATO mechanisms are being turned against the alliance members themselves,” the spokeswoman said.
Zakharova also accused Ukraine of creating security risks for Romania, citing an incident on August 20 in which a Romanian F-16 opened fire on an explosives-laden maritime drone near the Neptun Alpha gas platform in Romania’s exclusive economic zone.
Ukraine has escalated attacks in the Black Sea over the past several months. Ukrainian officials portray them as part of Zelensky’s much-hyped 40-day pressure campaign on Russia to end the conflict.
The Financial Times reported this month that Ukraine’s attacks drew the ire of the US, with Vice President J.D. Vance requesting that Zelensky halt raids on tankers serving the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal near Novorossiysk. The route mainly carries Kazakh crude and involves US majors Chevron and ExxonMobil. According to the FT, Kiev subsequently agreed not to target CPC infrastructure or non-Russian vessels unless they were sanctioned by Ukraine or are carrying Russian cargo.
In response to the campaign, Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s defense-related industry, vessels carrying military cargo, and port facilities in Odessa Region. The city is crucial for the country’s economy as it accounts for more than 90% of Ukraine’s seaborne exports, including agricultural products, which are the key source of income for the country.

articles.title: Pentagon wants Europe to take responsibility for its conventional defence and support for Ukraine
articles.body:
Pentagon wants Europe to take responsibility for its conventional defence and support for Ukraine
Elbridge Colby, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, has said that the United States expects Europe to take primary responsibility for its own conventional defence and a leading role in supporting Ukraine.
Source: Colby at NATO headquarters in Brussels on 27 August, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "We're actually having a kind of down to business conversation about how we go forward together in a world in which Europe, which is obviously a very wealthy continent, can and is taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defence. Obviously, the United States remaining committed to NATO, remaining linked to this alliance of course, and also Europe taking the lead in support to Ukraine."
Details: Colby said he wants to hear NATO allies' views on these positions.
He confirmed that the US had indeed sent a questionnaire to its European allies asking them to provide their assessments and plans regarding the future assumption of responsibility for Europe's conventional defence.
"We wanted allies to hear from them directly in writing, in the spirit of NATO 3.0 … which is a European-led conventional defence, but understanding how we manage across time, the extraordinary investments by governments like Poland, Germany, like your country, the Netherlands. And we hope others will come along," Colby said.
"Obviously, Europe remaining a critical interest of the United States even as we prioritise the Western Hemisphere," he stressed again.
The Pentagon official has also said that on the morning of 27 August in Brussels, he had "already had a series of really great meetings this morning with European counterparts". On 26 August, he received a briefing from the Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), while on 25 August, he visited US European Command together with General Alexus Grynkewich.
Background:

articles.title: Kremlin dismisses US media ‘scare stories’ on CIA chief’s Moscow visit
articles.body:
This file photo shows CIA Director Ratcliffe at a press conference.
The Kremlin Aug. 27 dismissed media speculation on the rare visit of the CIA director to Moscow earlier this week, after reports said U.S. intelligence chief John Ratcliffe warned Russia against attacking NATO.
“A lot of such scare stories are being published right now. Of course, they have nothing to do with reality,” said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, adding that Russia “is facing a very aggressive policy towards itself from European countries.”
Peskov’s remarks came after U.S. media reported on Aug. 26 that CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit was to warn Russia against any attack on NATO member states, after President Donald Trump sought to downplay the visit.
The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported Ratcliffe aimed to dissuade Russia from attacking NATO members amid U.S. intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance.
The Journal specified that Putin could test NATO with a “limited assault” in the next few years.
Trump said Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow on Aug. 25 was “semi-routine,” implying that the intelligence chief was in the Russian capital to discuss the Ukraine war.
“He’s there, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said in an interview with conservative radio host Glenn Beck.
Ratcliffe is one of the highest-ranking U.S. officials to visit Russia since its war with Ukraine started in 2022.
His visit came amid an escalation in Moscow’s offensive in Ukraine, with attacks this summer increasing the civilian death toll, while U.S.-brokered peace talks have stalled.
During his visit, Ratcliffe also discussed the war with Iran, warning of additional sanctions if the Strait of Hormuz doesn’t reopen to shipping traffic, CBS News reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.

articles.title: Russia-bound Turkish ship hit by drones – media
articles.body:
Russia-bound Turkish ship hit by drones – media
A Turkish-owned cargo vessel carrying fresh vegetables to Russia has been struck by drones in the Black Sea, leaving five crew members injured, according to Turkish media.
Ukraine intensified drone attacks on Russian commercial traffic in the Black Sea last month as part of a failed campaign intended to exert economic pressure on Moscow and force it to accept Kiev’s terms in the conflict.
The Cameroon-flagged Lider Bordo Mavi was struck by three drones off the Russian port of Tuapse, sparking a fire on board, according to Turkish media reports. Some news outlets suggested the overnight strikes were part of Kiev’s campaign against Russian maritime trade.
The ship belongs to a ten-vessel fleet operated by the Trabzon-based shipping company Lider Gida and departed the Turkish city port of Samsun on Tuesday. It was carrying fresh vegetables and had diverted to Tuapse from its original destination, the Russian port of Novorossiysk.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Novorossiysk, a major Russian Black Sea port, as well as commercial vessels using its facilities. Global shipping giant MSC suspended new bookings to and from the port earlier this week after one of its vessels was damaged in an attack, according to Bloomberg.
Türkiye “tested” by attacks on cargo ships
Erkut Celebi, head of the Trabzon Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the incident was the latest in a string of drone attacks on Turkish commercial vessels in the Black Sea and called on Ankara to provide financial support to affected companies.
“Türkiye is clearly being tested,” Celebi told reporters, warning that the attacks were threatening Black Sea trade and placing mounting pressure on Turkish exporters and shipowners.
Türkiye has remained largely neutral in the Ukraine conflict and maintained commercial ties with both Russia and Ukraine, drawing criticism from Kiev’s Western backers.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky announced the 40-day “pressure campaign” last month. Ukrainian forces targeted Russian oil refineries, civilian vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, and warehouses operated by commercial online retailers to pile up economic damage and inflict hardships on the Russian population.
Ankara played a major role in negotiating safe passage for ships through the Black Sea since the escalation of the conflict in 2022. The arrangement largely held, despite occasional attacks on vessels in neutral waters that Moscow attributed to Ukrainian operations.
Russian officials warned that Kiev was playing with fire by attacking other countries’ commercial vessels. After the latest escalation, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Kiev of opening Pandora’s box. Russian retaliatory strikes have effectively cut off shipments through Ukrainian Black Sea ports. Moscow has indicated that it does not intend to restore the previous arrangement.
“Our Turkish colleagues are once again proposing that some form of agreement be reached so that shipping is not subjected to attacks. Yet it was not us who initiated these hostilities,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.

articles.title: Israel escalates strikes on south Lebanon
articles.body:
ALBAWABA- Israel launched a new wave of airstrikes and artillery attacks across southern Lebanon on Thursday, while Israeli forces also carried out ground operations and demolitions, in what Lebanese authorities described as continued violations of the ceasefire and understandings governing the Israeli military withdrawal.
Israeli aircraft struck areas around Wadi al-Saluki, while artillery and airstrikes targeted several locations, including Mansouri, Meidoun, Zawtar al-Sharqiya and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, according to Lebanese reports. Israeli drones were also reported flying over parts of southern Lebanon. The attacks followed overnight and early-morning operations across several areas of the south.
In the Dabsh area near Mays al-Jabal, an Israeli force accompanied by tanks and bulldozers reportedly entered the area, burned homes and destroyed agricultural structures, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency. Israeli forces have also carried out demolitions and engineering operations in several southern towns in recent days.
The latest escalation comes as Israel and Lebanon remain engaged in negotiations over the implementation of security arrangements, including the deployment of the Lebanese army, the dismantling of Hezbollah’s military infrastructure and the eventual withdrawal of Israeli forces from areas Israel occupies in southern Lebanon.
The question of the Israeli withdrawal has become one of the most contentious elements of the process. Israel has indicated that its withdrawal will be conditional on verified action against Hezbollah, while senior Israeli officials have publicly signaled that the military intends to maintain a security presence in parts of southern Lebanon.
Earlier this month, Defense Minister Israel Katz said Israel would not withdraw from what he called the “security zone” and ordered preparations for a prolonged military presence. A senior U.S. official subsequently warned that a permanent Israeli military presence in southern Lebanon was inconsistent with the commitments reached under the emerging arrangements.
At the same time, Israel has intensified operations against what it allegedly describes as Hezbollah infrastructure. Israeli authorities say the strikes are aimed at preventing Hezbollah from rebuilding military capabilities and have linked some of the latest attacks to attempted drone attacks against Israeli forces. The Israeli military said Thursday that it had struck Hezbollah weapons-storage facilities in the Nabatieh area in response to two explosive drones launched toward its forces.
The escalation has also exposed growing tensions over the role of the Lebanese army. According to Israel’s Walla news outlet, Israeli officials have conveyed to Washington their dissatisfaction with the Lebanese army’s performance against Hezbollah infrastructure, arguing that Lebanese forces have failed to act effectively on locations identified by Israel. The report said Israel considers the current pilot arrangement in southern Lebanon to have failed.
Lebanon has meanwhile continued to demand an end to Israeli military operations and a full withdrawal, arguing that continued Israeli attacks undermine the ceasefire and prevent displaced residents from safely returning to their homes.
Lebanese authorities say Israel’s military campaign since March 2, 2026, has killed 4,350 people, wounded 12,307 and displaced more than one million.

articles.title: Video shows Ukrainian drone strike on Nebo-U radar at Russia's Millerovo airfield – photo

Drone operators from the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade have struck a Russian Nebo-U radar system at the Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast.
Source: 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade press service
Details: The attack was carried out by the brigade's long-range strike unit 170 km from the line of contact. The Russian military uses the Millerovo airfield to launch Shahed-type drones and other types of attack and decoy drones.
"This site is used to inflict aerial terror on the eastern, central and northern regions of Ukraine," the brigade explained.
The strike on the radar was carried out with a Ukrainian RAM-2X kamikaze drone.
The Russian Nebo-U three-coordinate VHF-band radar station is designed to detect and track aerial assets, including aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. The antenna height is 43 metres, and the radar's pulse power is 500 kW (average power 5 kW). The cost of the Nebo-U is estimated at US$100 million.
According to the brigade, the loss of the radar means that Russian forces will be unable to detect aerial assets in a timely manner within the station's operational zone.
Background: On the night of 12-13 August, a Russian Nebo-U radar station was struck in temporarily occupied Sevastopol.

articles.title: Poland not planning to host nuclear warheads, deputy defense minister says
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 27. /TASS/. Poland does not want and does not plan to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said.
"No - let me say it very clearly and openly. Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory," he told reporters at NATO headquarters in Brussels, as quoted by PAP. "We want to participate in NATO nuclear deterrence, which does not mean having nuclear warheads on our territory," Zalewski added.
President Karol Nawrocki said in an interview with Polsat in mid-February that Poland should field a nuclear arsenal. articles.title: GRU Involved in Sabotage Attempt Against An-124 Ruslan—U.S. Intelligence
articles.body:

On August 10, Die Zeit, based on an analysis of video footage, confirmed a failed sabotage attempt, during which the drone did not explode for unknown reasons.

articles.title: Russia’s number two online retailer reports drone attacks on logistics hubs in two regions
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked two Ozon logistics centers overnight on 27 August, one in Ufa and one in Orenburg Oblast, Russia's second-largest online store said. Staff were evacuated at both sites, and preliminary information indicated no casualties. Video published by Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ shows a drone reaching the Bashkortostan warehouse and exploding.
The strike on camera
Exilenova+ reported in the morning that an Ozon warehouse was burning after impacts in Blagoveshchensk, a town north of Ufa. The Bashkortostan capital lies roughly 1,300 kilometers from the war zone in Ukraine. Around midday the channel published eyewitness video of what it called the moment of a drone attack on the site, and said the warehouse had not caught fire. The footage shows a drone reaching the site and detonating there.
Earlier, the channel reported that residents of Sterlitamak, Bashkortostan's second-largest city, about 120 kilometers from Ufa, had written about explosions, with nothing then known about impacts. Astra later placed smoke over what it said was probably the Bashkir Soda Company works there.
Ozon said the Orenburg site—about 1,200 kilometers from the war zone—has resumed work. The one it placed in Ufa sustained what it called minor damage but remains closed, because the grounds need a thorough inspection. It is not accepting deliveries.
Russian news Telegram channel Astra identified the damaged facility from the eyewitness footage as Ozon's UFA_RFC fulfillment center in Blagoveshchensk. When it opened in late 2024 it was billed as the largest Ozon logistics complex in Russia's Volga federal district, with a total area of 93,000 square meters.
Smoke over the Ufa refineries
Astra also traced smoke in eyewitness footage to the Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim refinery in Ufa. The plant is one of Rosneft's leading refineries and a dual-use site: it supplies specialized fuel to Russia's armed forces and petrochemical feedstock for defense-grade materials. It burned after a strike on 1 August.
Ukrainian drones hit warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Ozon for the first time
What officials said, and didn't
Bashkortostan's authorities did not report the attack. Orenburg Oblast governor Yevgeny Solntsev mentioned drone danger in his region but gave no account of consequences. Ufa closed its airport.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed air defenses destroyed 267 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight across Russian regions, Bashkortostan among them.
The campaign so far
Ukraine's warehouse campaign began with Wildberries, Russia's largest online marketplace, which lost eight warehouses and roughly 860,000 square meters of storage in July alone. It reached Ozon for the first time on 22 August at Chapayevsk in Samara Oblast, where more than 500 employees evacuated and people were hurt. Four more Ozon hubs were hit across southern Russia two nights later.

articles.title: RAF and US fighters complete Combat Archer in UK
articles.body:
British and US combat aircraft have completed live-fire weapons evaluations during Combat Archer 2026, using more than 120,000 square kilometres of controlled training space around the Hebrides and Aberporth ranges.
RAF and US Air Force combat aircraft have completed a major air-to-air weapons evaluation exercise in the United Kingdom, with Typhoons, F-35s and F-15E Strike Eagles operating against unmanned and towed targets during Combat Archer 2026, according to the company.
The exercise was conducted across MOD Hebrides and MOD Aberporth, both operated by QinetiQ under the Long-Term Partnering Agreement with the Ministry of Defence. According to a QinetiQ news update, it was the first time the two ranges had been used together to support a single defence exercise, allowing the activity to make use of more than 120,000 square kilometres of air and surface space.
Participating aircraft included British Typhoon fighters, F-35Bs, F-35A Lightning IIs and F-15E Strike Eagles, supported by KC-135 Stratotankers from the US Air Force’s 100th Air Refuelling Wing. The evaluation itself was conducted by the Weapon System Evaluation Program team from the 83rd Fighter Weapons Squadron at Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida, where Combat Archer exercises are normally staged.
Combat Archer is designed to evaluate aircraft, weapons and crews under representative live-fire conditions rather than functioning solely as a conventional training exercise. The event allows participating units to employ weapons against realistic targets while specialists collect performance data from the aircraft, missile systems and supporting range infrastructure.
QinetiQ said its teams supported mission planning, preparation, range operation and specialist technical activity throughout the exercise. Staff at Hebrides and Aberporth were responsible for preparing and managing the large air and maritime operating areas required for live weapons activity while maintaining the safety arrangements needed to support multiple aircraft and target systems.
The exercise also involved QinetiQ teams from both the UK and Germany. A specially equipped PC-12 aircraft, registration D-FRMT, was used for maritime surveillance around the exercise area and to support flight safety before live-fire activity began.
Additional target presentation was provided by a PC-9B aircraft towing targets for participating fighter crews. QinetiQ Target Systems also supplied Banshee Jet 80+ unmanned aerial vehicles, which are designed and manufactured in Ashford, Kent. The combination of expendable unmanned targets and towed systems allowed crews to conduct weapons evaluations against different representative airborne threats.
Lee Rowe, Mission Rehearsal Lead at QinetiQ, said, as quoted in a news update: “Combat Archer 2026 highlights the unique range of capabilities that QinetiQ offers. The expertise of our teams in the United Kingdom and Germany has supported the US Air Force and the Royal Air Force in conducting realistic operational assessments, thereby strengthening interoperability between the air forces of the allies.”
He added: “We conduct complex exercises, thereby creating the necessary safety and reliability to maintain operational readiness and ensure that the armed forces are optimally prepared.”
The participation of the 83rd Fighter Weapons Squadron brought the US Air Force’s established weapons evaluation methodology to British ranges. The squadron’s Weapon System Evaluation Program assesses the effectiveness of aircraft and weapons during live employment, providing information on how crews and systems perform under more demanding conditions than can be reproduced through simulator training alone.
For the RAF, the event also provided an opportunity to train alongside US units operating different fighter types and support aircraft. The combination of Typhoon and Lightning aircraft with F-15Es, US F-35As and KC-135 tankers allowed crews to practise multinational procedures while the weapons evaluation element generated performance data from live activity.
Using Hebrides and Aberporth together was a significant range-management element of the exercise. QinetiQ said the combined area available was roughly equivalent to the size of England, giving planners sufficient space to conduct complex live-fire scenarios while coordinating aircraft, unmanned targets, surveillance assets and supporting range infrastructure.

articles.title: Trump says Russia’s Putin will not attack NATO territory, downplays Ratcliffe trip
articles.body:
Trump says Russia’s Putin will not attack NATO territory, downplays Ratcliffe trip
- President Trump said Russian President Putin will not attack NATO territory, reassuring there is no imminent threat.
- Trump downplayed reports about CIA Director Ratcliffe's trip to Moscow, stating no special message was delivered.
- US and European intelligence continue to monitor Russian grey-zone attacks aimed at weakening NATO unity and support for Ukraine.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump said on Aug 27 that Russian President Vladimir Putin will not attack a NATO country, and he played down media reports that CIA director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials against such an attack earlier in the week.
“He’s not going to attack a NATO territory,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Earlier in the day, Trump told Axios in a phone interview that there would be no such attack, and that Ratcliffe, who flew to Russia on Aug 25 to meet briefly with intelligence counterparts, had not been dispatched to deliver any particular message.
“Ratcliffe sees his Russian counterpart once every six months or once every year. They have a very good relationship. There was no message and there was nothing unusual,” Trump told the news outlet.
Trump’s comments came after the Wall Street Journal reported on Aug 26 that Ratcliffe had traveled to Moscow to warn Russia off any attack on a NATO member.
Two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters that Ratcliffe did bring up the possibility of a Russian operation against a NATO member during that meeting, though it was unclear if that was the sole purpose of the trip.
One source said they discussed several topics, including Russia’s support for Iran, which has proven an irritant for the US. The sources were granted anonymity to discuss US intelligence.
European and US intelligence officials have long monitored Russian sabotage and grey-zone attacks in Europe that fall below the threshold of full-on war and are generally aimed at weakening NATO’s unity and its member states’ willingness to support Ukraine against Russian aggression.
Among the potential plots that Western intelligence officials have been monitoring in recent months is the possibility that Russia uses a Ukrainian drone to attack a country in eastern or north-eastern Europe in a false flag operation that obscures Moscow’s authorship. REUTERS

articles.title: US Democrats increasingly oppose arming Israel: poll
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US Democratic voters are rapidly shifting on Israel, favour presidential candidate opposing arms
There has been a significant shift within the US Democratic Party towards Israel, according to a recent poll that found an overwhelming majority of Democratic voters in the first six states to hold presidential primaries in 2028 would support electing a presidential candidate who pledges to halt military aid to Israel and impose an arms embargo on it.
The poll by the Policy Project at the Institute for Middle East Understanding with YouGov surveyed about 4,000 likely voters in the Democratic primaries in South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia, with a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points.
The significance of the poll appears to lie in the fact that it extends to some states that do not have Arab and Muslim communities capable of influencing the course of elections, compared with the 2024 presidential election, in which Arab-American voters emerged as an influential bloc in states such as Michigan.
The results showed that most of Arab-Americans did not vote for presidential candidate Kamala Harris as punishment for her position on the genocide in Gaza. It also extends to states that predominantly vote Republican, such as South Carolina.
The shift in the general mood does not mean that this issue will determine the choice of the Democratic presidential candidate in 2028. But, it shows how Democratic voters view US military aid to Israel and the US position of providing it with unconditional support at the expense of Palestinian rights.
It should be noted that the party's presidential candidate is chosen through voters casting ballots for their preferred candidate in each state. Each candidate receives many delegates based on the proportion of votes they receive in each state, who pledge to support the candidate who selected them as delegates.
At the Democratic National Convention before the election, they vote to select the candidate. If no one secures a majority in the first round, senior delegates, including former presidents, state governors and members of Congress, vote in the second round. They account for about 15% of the delegates.
There are about 4,696 delegates to the party's national convention, including 3,949 pledged delegates and 747 known as senior delegates.
Some 75% of likely voters in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Michigan preferred a candidate who would prevent weapons from being sent to Israel, as did 74% in Nevada, 66% in Virginia and 65% in South Carolina.
Between 4% and 6% preferred a candidate who would send weapons to Israel.
Asked whether reducing US support for Israel would play a role in their vote, 65% of Michigan voters, 63% in New Hampshire, 61% in Nevada, 59% in New Mexico, 55% in Virginia and 46% in South Carolina answered "yes".
Some 70% in New Hampshire and New Mexico supported imposing US sanctions on Israel, compared with 68% in Nevada and Michigan, 61% in Virginia and 49% in South Carolina.
Meanwhile, 80% of likely voters in Michigan said they believed Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, compared with 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, 72% in Virginia and 57% in South Carolina.
Reasons behind the shift
In this context, Dr Edmund Ghareeb, a professor of political science at American University in Washington, DC, listed the reasons for the shift in Democratic voters' mood, foremost among them Israel committing genocide in Gaza, which was broadcast publicly on social media; its attacks on Lebanon; and its crackdown on the student movement on university campuses over Gaza.
"There has been a major change in the position of Democratic voters, particularly in states with Democratic majorities," Dr Ghareeb told TNA.
He noted that most Americans sympathised with Israel following 7 October 2023, when the Hamas-led "Al-Aqsa Flood operation" took place, but Israeli policies, attacks on civilians, the commission of genocide, attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, the expulsion of residents and Christians from their homes, and the destruction in southern Lebanon all contributed to changing the positions of Democrats and independents, according to Ghareeb.
He said the US administration's handling of university student protests over Gaza, the dispersal of those protests, the arrests of students, and restrictions imposed on the right to protest and freedom of expression all significantly affected how American society viewed the issue, particularly students and young people under 35.
He pointed out that the decline in support for arming Israel had extended to a proportion of American Jews, who had begun adopting positions against arming Israel that did not align with Democratic political leaders.
He cited New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani receiving 33% of the vote among New York Jews, adding that rising food and petrol prices and their impact on the middle and ordinary classes because of the US-Israeli war on Iran had also had a significant effect on both Democrats and Republicans.
Ghareeb warned that this change in public opinion may not last long if there is no effective organisation to capitalise on this shift in voters' views and if new currents within the Democratic Party, such as progressives, fail to make significant use of the change.
He said the Gaza issue and its spread on social media, as well as Israeli policies, had pushed progressives to change their positions, reject the genocide and benefit from the movement on US streets.
"We see a split within both the Democratic and Republican parties, and even if President Donald Trump has control over the Republican Party, he is losing between 20% and 25% of his overall supporters, which represents a severe blow to him," he said.
He attributed this to the presence of Republican figures who oppose wars, such as Thomas Massie, Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene.
