articles.title: Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic was unlawful, US judge rules
articles.body:
A US federal judge ruled Thursday that sanctions imposed in February by the Trump administration against AI giant Anthropic were illegal, finding that the government had punished the artificial intelligence company for publicly criticising the Pentagon.
“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Judge Rita Lin said in a 59-page decision.
She barred the federal agencies named in the lawsuit from enforcing President Donald Trump’s order to stop using the tools of Anthropic – creator of the Claude AI models – and overturned defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s designation of the company as a “supply chain risk”, a status previously reserved for foreign firms.
The ruling makes permanent the temporary suspension of sanctions ordered by the judge in March and takes effect immediately. The government may appeal.
“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said.
Hegseth’s unprecedented move, which followed Anthropic’s refusal to allow the military to use AI chatbot Claude for US surveillance or autonomous weapons, blocked Anthropic from certain military contracts. Anthropic executives have said it could cost the company billions of dollars in lost business and reputational harm.
Trump had lashed out at the company after its refusal, describing it in a February social media post as “a radical left, woke company” and “out-of-control”.
Anthropic says that AI models are not reliable enough to be safely used in autonomous weapons and that it opposes domestic surveillance as a violation of rights, but the Pentagon says private companies should not be able to constrain military action.
Anthropic’s designation was the first time a US company has been publicly designated a supply-chain risk under an obscure government-procurement statute aimed at protecting military systems from foreign sabotage.
Judge Lin, an appointee of Joe Biden, described the Pentagon’s designation as “illegal and baseless”.
In its 9 March lawsuit, Anthropic alleged the government violated its right to free speech under the first amendment of the constitution by retaliating against its views on AI safety. The company said it was not given a chance to dispute the designation, in violation of its fifth amendment right to due process.
The lawsuit says the decision was unlawful, unsupported by facts and inconsistent with the military’s past praise of Claude.
The justice department countered that Anthropic’s refusal to lift the restrictions could cause uncertainty in the Pentagon over how it could use Claude and risk disabling military systems during operations, according to a court filing.
The government said the designation stemmed from Anthropic’s refusal to accept contractual terms, not its views on AI safety.
Anthropic has a second lawsuit pending in Washington DC, over a separate Pentagon supply-chain risk designation that could lead to its exclusion from civilian government contracts.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: No signs Russia prepping military attack on NATO countries, says EU official
articles.body:
No signs Russia prepping military attack on NATO countries, says EU official
BRUSSELS - European intelligence agencies see no sign Russia is planning a military attack on European NATO countries, a senior EU official said on Aug 27, after US reports that the head of the CIA had warned Moscow not to strike the alliance.
Multiple US outlets reported that CIA director John Ratcliffe sought during a visit to Moscow to dissuade Russia from such an attack.
The Wall Street Journal reported it might seek to test NATO with a “limited assault” within a few years.
A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, played down the notion of an imminent risk.
“European services in general do not see any risk of an attack from Russia to the European countries, and this assessment has not changed,” said the official.
“When it comes to any threat to European NATO members, we see no assessment of any of that being under preparation now,” she added.
But she also said there was no doubt “Russia is trying actively to create difficulties for our countries”, with the European Union steadfastly backing Ukraine since the Russian invasion in 2022.
“This escalation by Russia is clearly there,” she said.
The EU has long called out what it considers “hybrid warfare” by Russia.
It has blamed Moscow for a lengthening list of incidents from drone incursions and cyberattacks to disinformation and political meddling, with eastern member states the most exposed.
“What we see is these hybrid and then not-so-hybrid attacks, which are continuing – and our assumption is that those will continue,” said the official.

articles.title: Syria's new army: Can Damascus build a truly national force?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria's new army: Can Damascus build a truly national force?
In late 2024, Syria’s army, exhausted by 14 years of war and stripped of much of its capacity, buckled as the state it served crumbled around it.
The force that had kept Assad in power for over a decade, with crucial backing from Russia and Iran, was unable to halt an offensive initially intended to push back the frontline, which then rapidly snowballed into an advance on the capital, Damascus.
In the aftermath of the overthrow of Assad, Syria's transitional government has set about rebuilding state institutions and a ruined country. This includes the Syrian army.
In the year and a half since, the transitional government, formed by the strongest rebel faction that spearheaded the collapse of Assad, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), has embarked on a journey to unify Syria's myriad factions into a professional, institutionalised force.
Yet, despite that effort, Syria's recent history has thrown up several stumbling blocks that weigh on the government's ability to create a coherent national force.
The HTS 'nucleus' of the new Syrian army
Like much of Syria's initial caretaker government, Syria's military formation has been centred on an HTS core, most notably represented by Murhaf Abu Qasra, the former head of HTS's military wing and now Syria's Defence Minister.
Qussai Jukhadar, a Syrian researcher, explained to The New Arab that this core was the result of two dynamics within HTS prior to Assad's fall: military discipline and institutionalisation.
"For example, violations against civilians in Idlib were very small in number compared, for example, to Afrin, which was controlled by the [Turkish-backed] national army," he said, adding that the national army factions would often fight each other.
"As an organisation, [Hayat Tahrir al-Sham] had a military college; it had artillery and tank specialisations; it had signal/communications; and it had military planning," Jukhadar added.
"So we can say that Hayat Tahrir al-Sham became the nucleus for the entire army."
Sixteen days after the collapse of the Assad regime, the new government announced the dissolution of all rebel factions and their merging into the Ministry of Defence following a series of discussions with rebel factions.
Unifying and professionalising the new army
On 29 January, a victory conference was held with the participation of an array of rebel factions that participated in the offensive against Assad, which saw the outlining of key policy positions, including a reaffirmation from all factions of their own dissolution into the state.
It was after this point that the factions decided on how to integrate into the state, which Jukhadar described as a "slow transition."
"They brought them in as factions, then they gave them numbers, then they placed brigade commanders and division commanders from Hayat Tahrir al-Sham over them, and then they started distributing specialisations to the military divisions," he told The New Arab.
This, alongside the weening out of veteran fighters for recruits, was aimed at homogenising the factions, moving them away from identities formed during the war.
Since then, Syria's government has undertaken numerous efforts to professionalise the army, including through international collaboration with its neighbour Turkey, which signed a bilateral defence agreement in August 2025 to help train, equip, and reform the new Syrian army.
This led to a batch of Syrian officer cadets travelling to Turkey for training, with Saudi Arabia also taking in cadets for training.
Its international partnerships have seen Syria's military coordinating with US Central Command in its shared mission against Islamic State (IS) cells in the country, and in May it took part in Turkey's bi-annual EFES multinational military exercises.
In March, al-Sharaa issued two presidential decrees establishing the Syrian University for Security Sciences and the National University for Defence Sciences. The latter integrated several institutions of military education, including the Higher Military Academy, the Air, Naval, and Military colleges, and the Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology, among others.
The move was aimed at further developing research and training programmes for Syria's officer corps, allowing for specialisation and establishing higher educational pathways.
However, Kheder Khaddour, a non-resident Scholar at the Malcolm H. Kerr Carnegie Middle East Center, said the importance of the new academies is yet to be determined, citing a lack of information on their resourcing or curriculum.
"They [the government] want a new Syrian army that's a professional army. But what is the doctrine of this army, what is the curriculum inside it? All of these are not clear, to be honest," he told The New Arab.
"What could be interesting here is who is going to train them," he added, noting that the academy and Syria's military are likely to have international partnerships that will define its doctrinal focus.
He cited Turkey, already a partner of Syria's military, Russia, Pakistan, the Gulf States, and Jordan as potentially influencing Syria's doctrine, with its posture towards both Israel and Iran also likely to be a determining factor in defining doctrinal questions.
The legacy of war: A confederal army, with local identities
Amid the ongoing effort to institutionalise the army, Khaddour noted several key dynamics from the war that have reemerged, stifling efforts to institutionalise the military factions into a unitary, national army.
"The Syrian military scene, from someone from outside receiving it like myself, is sort of a military confederation. This is what we see now," he said.
Khaddour explained that before the collapse of Assad, Syria's military personnel would serve away from their local areas, representing the nation and serving the state.
"It's necessary [that] the army must be a national army. A national army needs the officers to be outside their place of origin. Here what is happening is the opposite."
This is because Syria's myriad of armed factions, who had been displaced from across the country to the rebel-held northwest, returned to their local areas following the fall of Assad and set up roots, giving them local dimensions.
"This is the only way to prevent the collapse," Khaddour said, explaining that the country's fragility after Assad’s fall forced al-Sharaa's hand to allow armed factions to return to their localities, rather than deploying them elsewhere across the country to represent a national army.
"The dynamic of the returnees itself forced Sharaa to follow this approach."
The integration of units from the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which on Tuesday dissolved itself into the Syrian state, is also emblematic of this confederalism, Khaddour noted.
Although there is an integration process, with four Syrian army brigades being created from the SDF's military branch, these soldiers will be stationed in Syria's northeast, where the SDF previously governed.
"This is against the logic of a national central state," he said. "Instead of making a deal with SDF leaders to remain in their areas, you have to make a deal with them to be part of the Syrian military and to serve elsewhere."
Meanwhile, Syria's plethora of foreign fighters are being tightly controlled by Syria's military, according to Qussai Jukhadar, who told The New Arab that it “appears they are being moved around and distributed carefully so they are not grouped together with fighters from other factions".
"There is not much information about them, partly because they have not caused many problems. I also think this is deliberate, so as not to raise concerns among European countries and the United States."
Despite the presence and continued existence of local identities, Jukhadder said that the integration process was moving smoothly. "Even when disagreements arise, they are being resolved through dialogue," he told The New Arab.
This includes the removal of commanders from three formerly Turkish-backed Syrian National Army (SNA) units at the request of the Syrian Democratic Forces.
The commanders are under international sanctions following their human rights abuses during the war and fought battles against the SDF.
Yet, despite holding the factions together, creating a national institution is expected to take years, with Khaddour using the analogy of Syria's burgeoning officer corps as an example of the pace it will take.
"You need the military academy to graduate new officers, and if someone joined the military academy at 18 years old, until he becomes a mid-rank officer, he needs at least 10 years."
Looking ahead, Khaddour expects the local identities of Syrian factions to become stronger. "Time is not in the hands of Sharaa; it's in the hands of the factions, in the hands of locals."
Moving away from Assad's legacy
Yet, institutionalisation and professionalisation are essential for Syria's future stability.
In the immediate aftermath of the fall of Assad, two bouts of fighting, one on Syria's coast and the other in Suweida, saw sectarian massacres targeting Alawite and Druze civilians, with units of Syria's disparate army taking part.
Investigations from the government placed blame on lone personnel, citing a lack of institutional oversight, though a UN investigation described both incidents as being systematic.
Kholoud Helmi, a non-resident Fellow at TIMEP, told The New Arab that within Syria "there is a widespread desire for a military that protects the country and its people rather than the authorities".
She said that people wanted a military that is professional, politically neutral, accountable to civil authorities, reflects Syria's diverse community, and refrains from political involvement or acting as an internal security force.
"Above all, Syrians need to feel safe in the presence of the military, rather than threatened by it," Helmi said.
To do this, Syria's military needs a transparent vetting process to weed out those who committed crimes against humanity, alongside the integration of members of rebel factions as individuals rather than units, professional training on human rights law, and legal enforcement when those standards are broken.
Helmi also noted that the announcement of unification doesn't necessarily mean that a unified army exists, noting that alongside the retention of commanders, financial networks and ideological affiliations may also persist.
She identified two serious dangers for Syria’s future: military fragmentation leading to separate areas of control, and the concentration of power producing Assad-era practices.
"The real measure of reform is whether Syrians, regardless of their political position, ethnicity, religion or region, can encounter the military without fear of arbitrary arrest, humiliation, disappearance or retaliation."
Oliver Mizzi is a journalist at The New Arab

articles.title: Lavrov reveals what brought CIA chief and Vatican envoy to Moscow
articles.body:
Lavrov reveals what brought CIA chief and Vatican envoy to Moscow
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has addressed this week’s unusually intense diplomatic traffic in Moscow, shedding light on talks with the Vatican’s top diplomat while remaining deliberately vague about a visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Vatican’s Secretary for Relations with States and International Organizations, and Ratcliffe were both in the Russian capital this week, prompting RBK to ask Lavrov what was behind the visits.
“In both cases, those who came to us wanted to come and talk,” Lavrov said in an interview published on Friday.
Gestures of goodwill and broken promises
Lavrov said his discussions with Gallagher focused heavily on the Ukraine conflict, with the Vatican envoy reiterating a desire to see hostilities brought to an end as soon as possible and offering continued assistance on humanitarian issues, including prisoner and body exchanges.
The foreign minister used the meeting to recount a long series of diplomatic agreements broken, abandoned or derailed by Kiev and its Western sponsors – from the 2014 Euromaidan coup-era agreement to the Minsk accords used to buy Kiev time to rearm, and the 2022 Istanbul talks derailed by London.
“I pointed out that there had been no shortage of goodwill on our part... I think he understood everything. I would say he had no counterarguments, apart from the general slogan that ‘it needs to stop as soon as possible,’” Lavrov said.
Lavrov also told Gallagher that the Western push for a ceasefire along the current line of contact would merely freeze the fighting without producing a lasting settlement. Plans to deploy British- and French-led “stabilization forces” would effectively preserve the “neo-Nazi regime” in Kiev that suppresses the Russian language and the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church, he said.
Quiet intelligence channels
Lavrov was much more guarded about Ratcliffe’s visit.
“I wasn’t there,” he said, noting that intelligence agencies routinely communicate through established channels and that “there is nothing unusual” about such contacts taking place quietly. Diplomats, he added, also often work “in silence.”
“Of course, we do not disclose details that are too sensitive or are still being worked out, where it is important not to jeopardize possible compromises and consensus,” Lavrov said.
The top diplomat also denied allegations that Moscow had issued any kind of ultimatum to the administration of US President Donald Trump following media reports that American intelligence has been used to facilitate long-range Ukrainian strikes against Russia.
‘The end has already come’
Lavrov argued that Moscow remains willing to talk to Western governments but no longer assumes that public assurances or negotiated understandings will be honored.
“Deception is the basis of Western diplomacy. And it remains so,” he said, citing what Moscow regards as broken NATO assurances on expansion and successive derailed agreements over Ukraine.
Asked why Russia had continued to give its counterparts the benefit of the doubt, Lavrov said Russians tended to believe in people “until the very end.”
“But the end has already come,” he added, arguing that relations with the West would never return to what they were before February 2022.
What happened to Anchorage?
Lavrov presented last year’s presidential summit in Anchorage as the latest example of that frustration. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin went through a US peace proposal point by point with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who confirmed that it represented the American leader’s position. Putin then accepted the proposal despite some remaining “nuances,” according to Lavrov.
“If this is not consent and not an agreement, then I don’t know what an agreement is,” he said.
Washington disputes that characterization, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying in June that there had been “a proposal in Alaska, but there was no agreement.”
According to Lavrov, the Anchorage understandings were subsequently undermined over the following months by EU and British leaders. French President Emmanuel Macron eventually declared at the G7 summit in Evian in June that Anchorage had been “buried.”
Trump himself, however, has not explicitly declared the Anchorage framework dead. At the original August 2025 summit, he described the talks positively while cautioning that “there’s no deal until there’s a deal.”
Lavrov said Moscow remains ready to hear new US proposals, but in the meantime Russia will “continue working on the ground.”

articles.title: Drones attack thermal power plant in Shchastia, causing major blackout in Russian-occupied territories
articles.body:
Drones attack thermal power plant in Shchastia, causing major blackout in Russian-occupied territories
A major blackout occurred on the night of 27-28 August across temporarily occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. The power cuts followed a drone attack on the Luhansk Thermal Power Plant in the city of Shchastia.
Source: a Russian media outlet Astra; monitoring Telegram channels
Details: Local sources began warning of a possible drone attack as early as 21:00 on 27 August.
Around midnight, posts on social media about power outages began appearing in large numbers. In particular, the power went off in occupied Donetsk at around 01:00 on 28 August.
Local residents reported that the drone strike had caused a fire at the thermal power plant in Shchastia. Photos were also posted online that reportedly showed a fire at the facility.
Shortly afterwards, reports of widespread power outages began coming in from the so-called Donetsk People's Republic and occupied parts of Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. Meanwhile, local Telegram channels said there was "no precise or official information".
For reference: Russian forces fully occupied the city of Shchastia on 28 February 2022. After seizing the city, the Russians announced the so-called "nationalisation" of the power plant. They used the plant's generating units to cover the power shortfall in the so-called Luhansk People's Republic.
The Luhansk Thermal Power Plant is also a key facility supporting Russia's defence industry in Ukraine's east. The plant supplies electricity to military bases, repair facilities, coal mines and railway infrastructure used by the Russian military to supply its forces.

articles.title: Putin is not going to attack NATO territory — Trump
articles.body:
Putin is not going to attack NATO territory — Trump
Kyiv • UNN
The President of the United States denied that the CIA director was preparing a warning to Moscow. He also stated that Russia would not attack NATO.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin would not attack a NATO country and denied media reports that CIA Director John Ratcliffe had warned Russian officials earlier this week that such an attack was unacceptable, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"He is not going to attack NATO territory," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
It should be added
Earlier that same day, Trump said in a telephone interview with Axios that such an attack would not happen and that Ratcliffe had not been sent to Moscow to deliver any specific message.
"Ratcliffe meets with his Russian counterpart once every six months or once a year. They have a very good relationship. There was no message, and nothing unusual happened," Trump told the news outlet.
European and American intelligence services have long been tracking Russian sabotage and attacks in the "gray zone" of Europe, which do not reach the threshold of full-scale war and are generally aimed at weakening NATO unity and the readiness of member states to support Ukraine in its fight against Russian aggression.

articles.body:

Five Drones Breach Moldova’s Airspace as Russia Launches Overnight Attack on Ukraine
Five drones entered Moldova’s airspace without authorization overnight on August 27 following Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine, NewsMaker reported, citing Moldova’s Defense Ministry.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the report, the first drone crossed into Moldova from Ukraine at 3:56 a.m. near Biliaivka, flying toward Palanca in the Ștefan Vodă district. The aircraft subsequently left Moldovan airspace and returned toward Ukraine.
A second drone entered from the direction of Starokozache in Ukraine and was detected flying over the Moldovan village of Copceac at 3:59 a.m. It disappeared from monitoring systems at around 4:10 a.m. near Carahasani in the Ștefan Vodă district.
Nine minutes later, a third drone crossed the Moldovan-Ukrainian border and flew along a route toward Palanca, Crocmaz, Olănești, Purcari, and Răscăieți. At 4:24 a.m., the aircraft disappeared from radar near Pervomaisc in Moldova’s Transnistrian region.
A fourth drone entered Moldovan airspace at approximately 4:16 a.m. in the direction of Palanca before turning back toward Ukraine and heading toward the village of Maiaky.
The fifth incursion was recorded later in the morning, at around 5:50 a.m., near the Săiți-Lisne border crossing between Moldova’s Căușeni district and Ukraine. The drone crossed the border area before heading toward Lisne at 6:02 a.m. and leaving Moldovan airspace.
Moldova’s Defense Ministry linked the unauthorized incursions to Russia’s overnight aerial attacks on Ukraine.
Russian forces carried out a large-scale combined missile and drone attack across Ukraine overnight and into the morning of August 27, targeting multiple regions and repeatedly sending UAVs toward Kyiv.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia launched two Onyx anti-ship missiles from temporarily occupied Crimea, Iskander-M and North Korean-made KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Bryansk and Kursk regions, as well as 258 drones of various types.

articles.title: Military threat to Estonia from Russia unchanged after CIA chief's Moscow visit – Estonian Foreign Ministry
articles.body:
Military threat to Estonia from Russia unchanged after CIA chief's Moscow visit – Estonian Foreign Ministry
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna has said that CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow was nothing exceptional and that Estonia's assessment of the threat constantly posed by Russia has not changed.
Source: European Pravda, citing Tsahkna
Quote from Tsahkna: "We must remain vigilant, but Estonia's threat assessment has not changed. In recent years, NATO Allies have taken significant steps to strengthen collective defence and the Allies' defence capabilities. The best deterrent is a united and strong NATO and the clear understanding in Moscow that the Alliance is prepared to defend every inch of Allied territory."
Details: Tsahkna said the threat posed by Russia and potential provocations against NATO should be taken seriously, and that this is precisely what Alliance members are doing.
Throughout Russia's aggression against Ukraine, Tsahkna added, US officials have regularly met with Russian representatives, so the CIA director's visit should not be regarded as anything exceptional.
Quote: "Estonia is in close contact with all its Allies, including the United States. We exchange information and work to ensure that Russia understands NATO's unity and resolve in defending its territory."
Background:
- Politico reported that Ratcliffe had warned Russian officials during his visit to Moscow not to escalate tensions with US NATO allies, particularly Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
- On the morning of 26 August, US President Donald Trump rejected suggestions that Ratcliffe had made the trip to persuade Putin not to test NATO's resolve or attack the United Kingdom, which had pledged to step up its support for Ukraine that week. Trump described the visit as "semi-routine" but acknowledged that its purpose was to help end the war.
- The Kremlin, meanwhile, said that the CIA director's visit was related to contact between the Russian and US intelligence services.

articles.title: Russia attacks Kyiv Oblast, damaging warehouses in two districts and injuring two people
articles.body:
Russia attacks Kyiv Oblast, damaging warehouses in two districts and injuring two people – photos, video
Russian forces struck Kyiv Oblast with attack drones and ballistic missiles on the night of 26-27 August, damaging warehouses in the Boryspil and Fastiv districts. A 15-year-old girl and a 73-year-old woman have been injured.
Source: Tymur Tkachenko, Head of Kyiv Oblast Military Administration; Viktoriia Ruban, spokesperson for the Main Directorate of the State Emergency Service in Kyiv Oblast, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "The enemy attacked Kyiv Oblast with attack drones and ballistic missiles throughout the night.
Video: State Emergency Service of Ukraine
In the Boryspil district, the attack caused a fire at warehouses. Efforts to put it out are currently underway and all the necessary emergency services have been deployed at the scene."
Details: Warehouse facilities were also damaged in the Fastiv district. Houses were damaged in the Boryspil, Brovary and Vyshhorod districts.
A 15-year-old girl and a 73-year-old woman were injured in the Boryspil district. They received medical treatment at the scene and did not require hospitalisation.

Their work is being complicated by repeat Russian attacks. The threat of further strikes has forced firefighters to suspend their work several times and retreat to safer locations.
Background: Two educational institutions and a municipal medical facility have been damaged in Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi district and debris from downed aerial assets has landed between residential buildings in the Podilskyi district as a result of the latest Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital.

MOSCOW, August 28. /TASS/. Moscow has not issued any ultimatums to Washington regarding US assistance to Kiev in striking the territory of Russia; diplomats simply put forward a question to their US colleagues, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the RBC television in an interview.

articles.title: Iran could harm US economic interests in response to sanctions — security official
articles.body:
CAIRO, August 28. /TASS/. Iran could jeopardize US economic interests in the Middle East if Washington mounts its pressure of sanctions, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said.
"In the event of intensified US economic pressure on Iran, we will respond with countermeasures that will affect US interests in the region, " he told Lebanon’s Al Manar television channel without specifying the nature of these measures.
Rezaei added that, in his opinion, Washington’s shift toward economic pressure demonstrates that "a military solution to the conflict produces limited results."
The Axios portal reported on August 26 that Washington was not planning new attacks on Iran any time soon as it will focus on other means of pressure on Tehran, including sanctions.
The United States and Israel began their war with Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. articles.title: A lack of backbone! How jellyfish are taking over the world
articles.body:
In honor of the Guardian’s Invertebrate of the Year 2026 award — won by the leaf sheep, which isn’t even a sheep (the charlatan!) but rather a tiny neon green slug that lives underwater — this column is launching its own competition to find the most spineless creature in Europe.
The competition is open to all cowardly politicians and also actual invertebrates. Please write entries on a Post-it note and stick them on the bin outside Exki on the Schuman Roundabout.
Advertisement
Of course, calling a political opponent spineless or likening them to a jellyfish is a classic move. British politicians are particularly keen on this method of attack (a sting operation!). Conservative politician Michael Gove in 2024 likened Keir Starmer to a jellyfish, claiming he is “transparent, spineless and swept along by the tide.” He didn’t say whether Starmer also has only one hole used for both eating and expelling waste.
In 2008, David Cameron (who would go on to become the chinos-wearing assassin responsible for Brexit) said he’d seen “more spine in a bunch of jellyfish” than in then-Prime Minister Gordon Brown. Of course, as any good schoolchild knows, the collective noun for jellyfish isn’t “bunch” but “smack”. Yes, a smack of jellyfish (presumably because they are notorious heroin addicts).
Such a smack has been causing chaos in France this week, with jellyfish causing the partial shutdown of a nuclear reactor. Two of Gravelines nuclear power station’s six units were shut down because jellyfish were found in the seawater filtration system. And, despite not having brains (jellyfish, not the French!), the gelatinous creatures (again, we’re talking jellyfish, not the French) invaded the Gravelines plant on Aug. 11, 2025, and Aug. 11, 2026.
Rumors that these were Russian spy jellyfish sent on a mission to disrupt power flows in France were unconfirmed at the time of going to press. But can’t rule out Vladimir Putin using jellyfish for nefarious purposes.
A year ago, he and a Chinese ruler were caught on a hot mic musing about cheating death. “With the development of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Putin told Xi in a casual manner usually reserved for when you’re asking someone if they have plans for the weekend.
There is a type of jellyfish that has cracked living forever. Turritopsis dohrnii (also known as the immortal jellyfish) can reverse the aging process and revert from adulthood to being juvenile again.
Advertisement
It’s believed that the EU is hard at work harnessing the power of these jellyfish so that Maroš Šefčovič can remain a member of the College of Commissioners until the end of time.
CAPTION COMPETITION
“This will be a great addition to the German military. Sorry? This IS the German military?”
Thanks for all the entries. Here’s the best one from our mailbag — there’s no prize except the gift of laughter, which I think we can all agree is far preferable to cash or booze.

articles.title: Russia launched 140 drones against Ukraine over course of day, most targeting Kyiv
articles.body:
Russia launched 140 drones against Ukraine over course of day, most targeting Kyiv
                                        
                        —
                27 August, 19:46
                
                                        Stock photo: 153rd Mechanised Brigade
                                    
                                                        The Russian military launched around 140 attack drones, over 100 of which were jet-powered, on Ukraine during the day on 27 August.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Quote: "During the day on 27 August (from 07:00 to 19:00), Russian forces attacked Ukraine with approximately 140 attack drones (more than 100 of them jet-powered). The enemy directed the majority of the drones towards the Ukrainian capital.
Advertisement:
As of 19:00, more than 10 jet-powered attack drones remain in the airspace."
Details: Early data indicates that air defence systems shot down or jammed around 120 of the 140 attack drones during the day.
Background:
- On the night of 26-27 August, Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, two anti-ship missiles and 258 attack drones. Air defence systems neutralised 233 air assets.
- Since the start of the day on 27 August, the air-raid warning in Kyiv has been issued 11 times: air defence is engaging Russian drones, and a residential building has been damaged.
- Four people were injured in the Holosiivskyi district, and fires also broke out in the capital.
- Russian forces are also actively attacking Ukrainian warehouses containing products and other businesses. Russia destroyed a Roshen warehouse in the Boryspil district, damaged a distribution centre of the Comfy electronics store chain in Kyiv Oblast, and also destroyed a toy distribution centre.

articles.title: US and Canadian forces practise cruise missile defence
articles.body:
NORAD and US Northern Command are running Exercise Amalgam Dart across North America until 1 September, covering cruise missile defence scenarios and coordination with allied forces in the Arctic, the command stated.
The exercise began on 24 August and involves forces across the Alaskan, Canadian and Continental United States NORAD regions. According to the command, it is intended to sharpen the ability to detect, track, identify and respond to modern air domain threats.
American and Canadian personnel are integrating mixed fighter force operations, command and control organisations and air battle management, with aircraft flying as simulated adversaries. Training covers coordinated responses along both the eastern and western approaches to the continent, along with cruise missile defence scenarios using binational assets operating from 3 Wing Bagotville in Quebec.
The command describes the exercise as long-planned, routine and defensive.
That concept reflects a change in how the region is understood. NORAD was built around the shortest route between the Soviet Union and North America, which runs over the pole, and its warning and interception architecture faces north for that reason. The accession of Finland and Sweden to NATO has closed a gap on the European side of the same geography, and Russian long-range aviation operating from the Kola Peninsula presents a problem to both commands simultaneously rather than sequentially.
